Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend on their way to the airport calls, thinking they left their passport at home, and asks if you can check and bring it to them right away.
Situation2: They see a swimmer struggling near the middle of the pool and need to stay vigilant to respond quickly.
Story: I was sitting in the lifeguard chair, eyes scanning the pool, when my phone buzzed. It was Jamie, my best friend, in a panic. “I think I left my passport at home! My flight’s in two hours. Can you check and bring it to the airport? Please, I have no one else.” I could hear the desperation in their voice. As a friend, I knew I should help—Jamie would do the same for me. But as I looked up, I noticed a swimmer in the middle lane, their strokes faltering, head bobbing awkwardly above the water. My training screamed at me: never leave the pool unattended, not even for a minute. The safety of everyone here depended on my vigilance. My heart pounded as I gripped my phone, torn between the urgent call of friendship and the heavy responsibility of watching over the swimmers. Both roles demanded my immediate attention, but I couldn’t possibly fulfill them at the same time.
